assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints that amplify and propagate shocks are a foundational mechanism in modern macroeconomics. Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 'Credit Cycles' framework underlies much work on financial frictions, macro-finance and crisis analysis. It is a clear conceptual advance with broad downstream use in policy and quantitative models.
assessment.attribution: The collateral-constraint dynamic amplification mechanism is clearly credited to Kiyotaki and Moore. Gertler and Gilchrist are linked to the financial-accelerator strand. That strand overlaps with prior recognition of the Bernanke-Gertler framework, so I would not extend the proposal to them.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades have passed. The ideas are thoroughly vetted, widely taught and embedded in central-bank and academic models, so there is no timing concern.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee sees the financial-accelerator area as already partly covered by the 2022 prize (Bernanke) and wants a distinct contribution.
The relative weight of Kiyotaki-Moore versus the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist strand. This is my own judgement and I have not verified it independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology, skill-biased change and polarization, together with the empirical work on trade shocks, reshaped understanding of wages, inequality and local labour-market adjustment. It has very high policy relevance and has influenced both labour and trade economics.
assessment.attribution: Katz is credited for the skill-demand and education-race strand. Autor is credited for the task and polarization approach and, with Dorn and Hanson, for the China shock. The three-laureate limit forces a choice, and Dorn is the most plausible omission. The theoretical task framework also owes much to Acemoglu, who is not listed on this ballot and has already been recognised.
assessment.maturity: The core papers span roughly 1992 to 2013, and the China-shock literature has had a decade of replication and debate. It is mature, though the long-run interpretation of the shock effects is still being refined.
uncertainties: Debate over the magnitude and persistence of the China shock effects.
Overlap with the 2024 prize on technology and institutions and with trade-economics recognition.
Choice among Autor, Dorn, Hanson and Katz.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Misallocation of inputs across firms is a leading explanation of cross-country income differences. It built a bridge between firm-level microdata and aggregate productivity and has driven a large research agenda in macroeconomics and development. It is a major, measurable quantitative contribution to understanding growth.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the central paper. Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) is the parallel theoretical contribution, and Rogerson is not listed on this ballot. Restuccia's agricultural-productivity work is a strong complement, but the credit split is delicate.
assessment.maturity: About 15 to 18 years of citations, replication and extensions, including critiques of measurement. It is mature enough.
uncertainties: Disclosure: Klenow is a long-running co-author of mine, so my assessment may be biased and should be weighed accordingly.
Measurement-error critiques of the misallocation estimates.
Absence of Rogerson from the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: HANK models changed how monetary and fiscal transmission is analysed by showing that heterogeneity in marginal propensities to consume matters for aggregate policy effects. They also provide tools for combining micro data with general equilibrium. The contribution is conceptually and methodologically significant and highly influential.
assessment.attribution: Kaplan, Moll and Violante (2018) is the clear anchor, and the three credited names fit the three-laureate limit. The broader heterogeneous-agent tradition draws on earlier work such as Aiyagari, Huggett, Krusell-Smith and Bewley, which complicates attribution of the field as a whole.
assessment.maturity: The key paper is from 2018. The framework is widely adopted but young, and long-run empirical validation and policy track record are still developing.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee considers it too recent.
Dependence on foundational earlier heterogeneous-agent work with which the proposed laureates may be compared.
Disclosure: I have co-authored with colleagues in the heterogeneous-agent literature, though not with these three.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm trade framework showed how trade liberalization reallocates activity toward more productive firms, creating gains beyond classical and new-trade-theory channels. It reoriented empirical and theoretical trade research and links to firm-dynamics themes in macro.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the pivotal contribution. Helpman has a long record on trade with increasing returns and firm heterogeneity, and Redding contributed quantitative spatial and trade applications. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum (2003) are an important parallel contribution that is not credited on this ballot.
assessment.maturity: Over 20 years of work, so it is mature. Quantification of the gains from trade has been refined, with debate over how much firm heterogeneity changes aggregate welfare predictions.
uncertainties: Omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum from the credited set.
Krugman's 2008 prize partly covers adjacent trade theory.
Whether the aggregate welfare implications differ materially from simpler models.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Measuring intergenerational mobility with population-scale administrative data transformed the empirical study of opportunity. It exposed geographic variation and causal neighbourhood effects and has had unusual public and policy impact. The data-driven method has set a new standard in public and labour economics.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure across the project. Hendren is credited for the neighbourhood-effects and mobility-estimation work and Friedman for the tax-data infrastructure and teacher-value-added work. Katz's credit is mainly for the Moving to Opportunity studies. The team-based project makes credit allocation hard.
assessment.maturity: The core results date from about 2014 to 2022. Replication and extension are ongoing, and some causal-interpretation claims are still debated.
uncertainties: Relative youth of the evidence base.
Team-based attribution and large-scale data-access conditions.
Debate on causal neighbourhood effects and on measurement of mobility.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities, built on Calvo pricing, provides the standard theory of monetary policy used by central banks worldwide. Its normative implications for inflation targeting and policy rules are very influential, though the apparatus is less novel than it was two decades ago.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is the main difficulty. Calvo contributed staggered pricing, Woodford the integrated policy framework, and Gali (with Clarida and Gertler) the canonical estimation and policy formulation. Taylor, Rotemberg, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Wouters also have strong claims. Three names cannot capture the field.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with decades of use and an extended track record. The post-2008 and post-2021 inflation episodes have prompted reassessment, which tests robustness without undermining the contribution.
uncertainties: Fragmented credit across many contributors and Rotemberg's absence from the list.
Continuing critiques of the framework, including the role of heterogeneity.
Whether the field is better recognised via a different laureate combination.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Methods for structural estimation of demand in differentiated-product markets and for dynamic industry models turned industrial organization into a quantitative tool for merger analysis, market-power measurement and policy evaluation. They are widely used across applied microeconomics and antitrust practice.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (1995, BLP) is the anchor contribution for demand estimation, and Pakes also contributed to dynamic models and to production-function and entry work. Bresnahan, Reiss and others have strong claims for the earlier empirical-IO tradition, and Ericson-Pakes and Benkard are separate dynamic strands. The credit set is large and diffuse.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use, so very mature. Methodological refinements and concerns about identification and computational reliability continue.
uncertainties: Diffuse attribution across empirical IO, with Bresnahan and Reiss as alternative or additional candidates.
Whether the Committee views the contribution as methodological rather than a discovery.
Sensitivity of BLP estimates to implementation and instruments.
